Trump’s DOJ probes major TV networks over response to White House ban of CNN
Jaguar reveals a $130,000 all-electric vehicle. Why?
Jeff Kizer doesn’t equate money with happiness. But his future concerns him.
A television camera outside the West Wing of the White House on September 21, 2026. Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg/Getty Images/File Media Donald Trump Federal agencies Human rights See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! Follow The Justice Department is investigating the five major US TV networks for possible antitrust violations, opening yet another front in the Trump administration’s pressure campaign against the press.
The probe, which one leading First Amendment group called nonsensical, concerns the TV pool, a long-standing arrangement that was disrupted last month when President Donald Trump banned CNN from the White House grounds. The pool is a small, rotating group of journalists that provides coverage of the president and represents the larger press corps.
The TV pool chair at the time said that with Trump “preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties,” there would be “no replacement pool put in place.”
There was no pooled TV coverage of Trump’s events for several days until a federal judge issued an order temporarily halting Trump’s ban on CNN, MSNOW and Politico. That litigation is ongoing, and the Justice Department is defending Trump’s action in court.
Now, the Justice Department is also probing how the TV pool functions. The highly unusual inquiry was first reported by The New York Times on Saturday. It comes two weeks after Trump ally Laura Loomer publicly encouraged the DOJ to challenge the networks on antitrust grounds.
In a statement to CNN, a Justice Department spokesperson confirmed the contours of the investigation.
“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” the spokesperson said. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”
Representatives for the five networks that have made up the pool for decades — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC — either declined to comment or did not respond to requests for comment on Saturday night.
Bruce D. Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said the investigation “appears to be a pretext for seeking records from the networks about how they are covering daily White House events during a media ban the president himself put in place.”
Brown added, “The decisions news organizations make about coverage are protected by the First Amendment, and summoning antitrust authority, on top of the retaliatory actions the White House has already taken to bar certain outlets, is another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.”
Some of the networks first learned about the investigation on Friday, two sources with knowledge of the matter said, when attorneys for the networks received government demands for documents relating to the pool, including its formation and its recent operations.
Through the pool, the five TV networks take turns documenting the president’s appearances, sharing live and taped footage with one another and the wider press corps. It’s a costly 365-day-a-year endeavor, with multi-day trips often costing tens of thousands of dollars for the networks involved.
The TV pool system emerged out of necessity back in the era of the three broadcast networks. It enables a single TV crew to provide presidential event coverage for many news organizations when space or access is limited.
Viewers worldwide are the beneficiaries. For example, presidential Q&As in the Oval Office and trips on Air Force One are typically covered by the pool. Local TV stations, newspaper websites and media outlets worldwide rely on the footage.
Jonathan Kanter, the Biden administration’s assistant attorney general for antitrust, said any antitrust-violation claims will run into Supreme Court precedent that upheld civil rights-era boycotts as protected speech.
“This is not even in the same zip code of an antitrust violation,” Kanter told CNN. “It’s literally freedom of speech.”
The press pool coming together is a First Amendment-protected freedom, Kanter said. He noted that the press pool has existed for years, with cooperation from successive White Houses. Pool members cooperating in response to what they believe to be a First Amendment violation by the administration cannot suddenly become an antitrust issue.
“It’s no more an antitrust violation than the reporters coming together to form the pool in the first place,” Kanter said.
When Trump’s ban of CNN disrupted the pool operation, the five networks issued a rare joint statement that read, “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
The pool’s decision to stand with CNN — rather than put a replacement pool in place — was described in an email by Bryan Boughton, the Washington bureau chief for Fox News, who was the TV pool chair at the time.
Chloe Arensberg, the DC bureau chief for NBC News, is now the TV pool chair.
One of the sources with knowledge of the matter said the Justice Department probe may factor into the lawsuit CNN and the two other banned outlets, MS NOW and Politico, filed last month.
Alleged retaliation against the news outlets has been a throughline in the legal filings by lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
The Freedom of the Press Foundation reacted to the news of the probe Saturday night by saying, “What nonsense.”
“Trump may view the presidency as a business venture, but news outlets’ standing up for the First Amendment has nothing to do with antitrust law,” the advocacy group wrote on Bluesky.
Nico Perrino, an executive vice president at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, invoked Trump’s inauguration day pledge to restore free speech and said the probe was another example of retribution.
“Is there a lever this administration is unwilling to pull to punish its enemies?” Perrino wrote on X. “So much for ‘bringing free speech back to America’ and ending the lawfare.”
